explanation: Climbing fibers are the axons of contralateral inferior olivary nucleus neurons. They ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle and climb on Purkinje cell dendrites. They carry error signals for motor learning. Mossy fibers (not climbing) end in granular layer.
keyConcept: Climbing fibers: olivocerebellar (contralateral ION), climb on Purkinje dendrites, carry error signals.

explanation: Climbing fibers travel via the olivocerebellar tract through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum. The dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the trunk. The pontocerebellar tract carries mossy fibers from the pontine nuclei.
keyConcept: Olivocerebellar tract: inferior cerebellar peduncle → climbing fibers to cerebellum.

explanation: The molecular layer of cerebellum contains stellate cells (with cell bodies here), basket cells (with cell bodies here), and the dendrites of Purkinje cells and Golgi cells. Purkinje cell bodies are in the Purkinje layer. Golgi cell bodies are in the granular layer. Cerebellar glomeruli are in the granular layer.
keyConcept: Cerebellar molecular layer: stellate + basket cells, Purkinje/Golgi dendrites. Purkinje layer: Purkinje cell bodies. Granular layer: granule cells, Golgi bodies, glomeruli.

explanation: The cerebellar cortex has 3 layers: molecular layer (outer), Purkinje cell layer (middle), and granular layer (deepest/innermost). The granular layer contains granule cells, Golgi cells, and cerebellar glomeruli.
keyConcept: Cerebellar cortex layers (superficial to deep): molecular → Purkinje → granular.

explanation: In pyramidal cells, the APEX (where the thick branching dendrite arises) is directed INWARD toward the white matter, and the BASE is directed toward the cortical surface. The axon emerges from the base. Betz cells are indeed giant pyramidal cells in the motor cortex.
keyConcept: Pyramidal cell orientation: apex (dendrite) faces inward (white matter); base (axon) faces outward (surface).

explanation: Purkinje cells are characteristic of the CEREBELLAR cortex, not cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex has 6 layers: molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, internal pyramidal, and multiform. The cerebellar cortex has 3 layers.
keyConcept: Cerebral cortex layers: I-VI (6 layers). Cerebellar cortex: molecular, Purkinje, granular (3 layers).

explanation: All of these - pyramidal cells, granular cells, fusiform cells, and Martinotti cells - ARE cells of the cerebral cortex. Pyramidal cells are the most common excitatory neurons. Granular cells are small interneurons. Fusiform cells are in the deep layer. Martinotti cells have ascending axons.
keyConcept: Cerebral cortex neurons: pyramidal (main), granular, fusiform, Martinotti, basket, Chandelier cells.

explanation: The outer band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL GRANULAR layer (layer IV). This band represents dense termination of thalamocortical fibers. The inner band of Baillarger is in the internal pyramidal layer (layer V).
keyConcept: Outer Baillarger: layer IV (internal granular) - thalamocortical input. Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal).

explanation: The inner band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V), which contains Betz cells in the motor cortex and other pyramidal neurons. The horizontal myelinated fibers form this band.
keyConcept: Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal) - contains Betz cells and corticospinal neurons.

explanation: Astrocytes contain microtubules (for transport), GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein - their intermediate filament marker), and thread-like mitochondria. These contents help identify astrocytes histologically. GFAP is the most specific marker.
keyConcept: Astrocyte cytoplasm: GFAP (marker), microtubules, mitochondria. GFAP used for astrocyte identification.

explanation: Microglia are present in CNS including retina and optic nerve (CNS outgrowths). They are small spindle-shaped cells with branching poles and fine spines on their surfaces. They are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm.
keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages, spindle-shaped with branched spiny processes, mesodermal origin.

explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) exits the brainstem between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle, at the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla. This is the same level where glossopharyngeal and accessary nerves also emerge.
keyConcept: Vagus nerve: exits between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle at posterolateral sulcus.

explanation: GSA (general somatic afferent) fibers of the facial nerve carry proprioception from facial muscles and sensation from a small area of the external ear. These fibers relay in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, which spans the pons and medulla.
keyConcept: Facial nerve GSA: relays in spinal nucleus of trigeminal (same as other facial sensation).

explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) has ONLY general somatic efferent (GSE) fibers, supplying the extrinsic and intrinsic muscles of the tongue. Other cranial nerves have mixed components. The vagus, glossopharyngeal, and accessory nerves all have visceral components.
keyConcept: CN XII (hypoglossal): only GSE fibers to tongue muscles. Vagus: GSE + GVE + SVA + GVA.

explanation: The spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is equivalent to substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II) of the spinal cord dorsal horn. Both are involved in pain and temperature transmission. The main sensory nucleus handles fine touch; Clarke's nucleus is for proprioception.
keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of V = substantia gelatinosa (pain/temp). Main sensory nucleus = epicritic touch.

explanation: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the vagus. The vagus has: nucleus ambiguus (branchial GSE), dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (GVE), and solitary nucleus (SVA, GVA).
keyConcept: Vagus nuclei: nucleus ambiguus (motor), dorsal motor nucleus (parasympathetic), solitary nucleus (sensory).

explanation: The abducent nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle, close to the midline in the lower pons. It supplies the lateral rectus muscle. The facial motor nucleus is more lateral, and the hypoglossal nucleus is in the medulla.
keyConcept: Abducent nucleus: floor of 4th ventricle, lower pons, near midline; supplies lateral rectus.

explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the ONLY cranial nerve that decussates (crosses) before emerging from the brainstem. It decussates in the superior medullary velum. All other cranial nerves emerge without crossing.
keyConcept: CN IV (trochlear): only cranial nerve that decussates before emergence; crosses in superior medullary velum.

explanation: Internal arcuate fibers (crossing fibers from gracile and cuneate nuclei) are present in the CLOSED MEDULLA where they sweep around the central gray to form the medial lemniscus. In the open medulla, these fibers have already crossed and ascended.
keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers: cross in closed medulla, sweep around central gray to form medial lemniscus.

explanation: The main inferior olivary nucleus is present in the OPEN (not closed) medulla, located ventrolaterally. The closed medulla contains: motor decussation (lower), sensory decussation (higher), gracile and cuneate nuclei and tracts.
keyConcept: Closed medulla: decussations, gracile/cuneate nuclei. Open medulla: inferior olivary nucleus.

explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) emerges from the PONS (at pontomedullary junction), not the medulla. The medullary cranial nerves are: IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal).
keyConcept: Medullary cranial nerves: CN IX, X, XI, XII. CN VII (facial) is pontine.

explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are present on the DORSAL aspect of the closed medulla, forming the tubercles seen on the posterior surface. These nuclei receive proprioception and fine touch from the lower and upper body respectively.
keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate nuclei: dorsal closed medulla; receive proprioception and fine touch.

explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are the DECUSSATING (crossing) fibers of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal system. They cross in the sensory decussation of the closed medulla and form the medial lemniscus. External arcuate fibers are cerebellar afferents.
keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers: cross in sensory decussation → form medial lemniscus. External arcuate: cerebellar afferents.

explanation: The lowermost medulla (near spinomedullary junction) shows the DECUSSATION OF CORTICOSPINAL FIBERS (motor decussation). The pyramids are not yet formed. The inferior olivary nucleus appears at higher (open medulla) levels. Superior olive is pontine.
keyConcept: Corticospinal decussation: lowermost medulla (motor decussation). Sensory decussation is higher. Olivary nucleus is higher still.

explanation: The arcuate nucleus is found VENTRAL to the pyramids, in the anterior median fissure. It is a relay nucleus in the corticocerebellar pathway. It receives input from the cortex and projects to the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Arcuate nucleus: ventral to pyramids, in anterior median fissure; pontocerebellar relay.

explanation: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from the ARCUATE NUCLEUS (not the cuneate nucleus which projects to cerebellum via dorsal external arcuate fibers). The arcuate nucleus receives corticofugal fibers and projects to the cerebellum.
keyConcept: Ventral external arcuate: from arcuate nucleus → cerebellum (via ICP). Dorsal external arcuate: from accessory cuneate → cerebellum.

explanation: The accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus gives rise to UNCROSSED fibers that ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum (cuneocerebellar tract). These carry proprioception from the upper limb.
keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus: uncrossed fibers → cerebellum via ICP; proprioception from upper limb.

explanation: The central gray (around the central canal) in the upper closed medulla contains the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. At this level, it is continuous with the spinal nucleus in the medulla. The nucleus solitarius is more lateral.
keyConcept: Central gray upper medulla: spinal nucleus of V. More laterally: nucleus solitarius. Ventrally: inferior olivary nucleus.

explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in the UPPER level of closed medulla where the sensory decussation occurs. At the lower level, the motor decussation is occurring. In the open medulla, the medial lemniscus has already formed and ascended.
keyConcept: Upper closed medulla: sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers). Lower closed medulla: motor decussation.

explanation: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system through its extensive connections with the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is the main link between the nervous system and the endocrine system, and the reticular formation modulates hypothalamic function.
keyConcept: Reticular formation → hypothalamus → pituitary → endocrine control. RF also influences autonomic functions via hypothalamus.

explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus receives input from the red nucleus (rubro-olivary fibers). It is located in the OPEN medulla, not ventral aspect. Its efferent fibers decussate and reach the CONTRALATERAL cerebellar cortex through the INFERIOR cerebellar peduncle as climbing fibers.
keyConcept: Inferior olivary: receives rubral input, in open medulla, projects via ICP to contralateral cerebellum as climbing fibers.

explanation: The superior olivary nucleus is a relay in the auditory pathway, located in the pons. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei and projects to the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus. The trapezoid body also passes through this area.
keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive (binaural hearing) → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB.

explanation: Sections at the lower level of pons show the MIDDLE cerebellar peduncle (the largest cerebellar peduncle, connecting pons to cerebellum). The superior cerebellar peduncle is more superior. The mesencephalic nucleus of V is in the midbrain. Medial and inferior vestibular nuclei are in the upper medulla.
keyConcept: Lower pons: middle cerebellar peduncle. Midbrain: superior cerebellar peduncle. Medulla: inferior cerebellar peduncle.

explanation: Basis pontis contains corticospinal fibers (descending to spinal cord), corticonuclear fibers (to cranial nerve nuclei), and transverse pontine fibers (to cerebellum). Pontine reticulospinal fibers are in the tegmentum (not basis), along with other tegmental structures.
keyConcept: Basis pontis: corticospinal, corticonuclear, transverse pontine fibers. Tegmentum: reticulospinal, sensory nuclei.

explanation: The medial lemniscus carries somatosensory information (fine touch, vibration, proprioception), not auditory information. Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex.
keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB → auditory cortex.
